paragraphs.text: Made, say Vatablus and others, at that time when Saul pursued David in the wilderness of Maon, 1Sa 23:24. But by many circumstances and passages of this psalm it appeareth more probable that it was, as the former, composed when Absalom was up, 2Sa 15:10-12 Sss Psa 31:11-12; Psa 31:22 of this psalm, with 2Sa 17:24; 2Sa 17:27; 2Sa 19:33; Joseph. Antiq. lib. 7, cap. 9.
paragraphs.anchor: A Psalm of David

paragraphs.text: Hic Psalmus varia mixtus et magna effectuum vicissitudine insignis est. This psalm is strangely mixed and made up of many and divers passions and petitions, according to the change of times and estate. In the time of affliction he prayeth, in the time of consolation he praiseth the Lord, Ecc 7:15. In these three first verses is little said but what had been before said, and is already opened.
paragraphs.anchor: In thee, O Lord, do I put my trust

paragraphs.text: i.e. Repulsed, worsted, defeated.
paragraphs.anchor: Let me never be ashamed

paragraphs.text: And not according to mine own righteousnes, saith Kimchi, or, according to thy faithfulness.
paragraphs.anchor: In thy righteousness

paragraphs.text: This repetition of his petition is no vain babbling, as Mat 6:9, but an effect and an evidence of greatest earnestness, as Mat 26:44.
paragraphs.anchor: Bow down thine ear to me, deliver me

paragraphs.text: Where the enemy can as little hurt me as when I was in the hold, 1Sa 22:4.
paragraphs.anchor: For an house of defence

paragraphs.text: Such places David had been forced to fly to; but still he trusted in God.
paragraphs.anchor: For thou art my rock and my fortress

paragraphs.text: Duc me, et deduc me. A metaphor from captains and generals, who lead on their armies with greatest art and industry (Vatab.).
paragraphs.anchor: Lead me, and guide me

paragraphs.text: That noted net, as the Hebrew hath it; Nam Zu denotat rem notam omnibus, saith Kimchi. David was not caught in it; but the enemies presumed he would be, so selling the hide before the beast was taken; as did likewise the proud Spaniards, when, coming against England in 1588, they triumphed before the victory, and sang,
paragraphs.anchor: Pull me out of the net

paragraphs.text: Tu quae Romanas suevisti temnere leges,
Hispano disces subdere cells iugo.
But blessed be God, the net brake, and we escaped, Psa 124:7.

For thou art my strength] As a tree is strongest at the root, and a branch or bough next the trunk or stock, and the farther it groweth out from thence the smaller and weaker it groweth too; so the nearer the creature is to God the stronger; and on the contrary.

So did our Saviour, so did St Stephen, and divers of the dying martyrs, with these very words, most apt and apposite surely for such a purpose. But what a wretch was that Huberus, who died with these words in his mouth, I yield my goods to the king, my body to the grave, and my soul to the devil.
paragraphs.anchor: Into thine hand I commit my spirit

paragraphs.text: And so hast best right unto me.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast redeemed

paragraphs.text: I know whom I have trusted.
paragraphs.anchor: O Lord God of truth

paragraphs.text: i.e. Idols, or aught else besides the living God, who giveth us all things richly to enjoy, 1Ti 6:17 Jon 2:8. {See Trapp on "Jon 2:8"} Vanitates vanitatis, Vatablus rendereth it, and telleth us that some understand it of astrology. R. David doth so in this note of his upon the text, Astrologos et incantatores in fuga mea non consului, sed in Domino et prophetis eius confisus sum; I have not consulted astrologers and soothsayers in my trouble, but have trusted to the Lord and his prophets.
paragraphs.anchor: I have hated them that regard lying vanities

paragraphs.text: In the midst of trouble faith will find matter of joy; as extracting abundance of comfort in most desperate distresses from the precious promises and former experiences.
paragraphs.anchor: I will be glad and rejoice

paragraphs.text: God knows our souls best, Psa 1:6, and we know him best, in adversity. Isa 63:16, the Church thought she should know him in the midst of all his austerities.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast known my soul in adversity

paragraphs.text: i.e. Not given me into their power. See Psa 27:12.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast not shut me up, &c.

paragraphs.text: So that I can freely and fearlessly go in and out. See Psa 25:15.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast set my feet in a large room

paragraphs.text: Antiquum obtine, Do now, Lord, as thou hitherto hast done.
paragraphs.anchor: Have mercy upon me, O Lord

paragraphs.text: Overwhelmed with the terrors of death, and ready to sink, animus mihi pendet, I know not what to do.
paragraphs.anchor: For I am in trouble

paragraphs.text: Computruit facies mea, mine eye ( nitor oculi, vel facies) is gnawn away, or worm-eaten.
paragraphs.anchor: Mine eye is consumed with grief

paragraphs.text: Belly may be taken for the whole body, which was pined away and infeebled with pensiveness. Vatablus by soul understandeth the natural appetite after meat, and by belly the digestion, both which were decayed.
paragraphs.anchor: Yea, my soul, and my belly

paragraphs.text: Which threateneth the thread of life, and soon snappeth it in sunder, 2Co 7:10. See Pro 17:22; Pro 17:25. {See Trapp on "Pro 17:22"} {See Trapp on "Pro 17:25"}
paragraphs.anchor: For my life is spent with grief, &c.

paragraphs.text: So that I stumble and stagger, Psa 27:2.
paragraphs.anchor: My strength faileth

paragraphs.text: Or, my misery; for sin hales misery at the heels of it; and the Scripture often confoundeth the names of the cause and of the effects.
paragraphs.anchor: Because of mine iniquity

paragraphs.text: Heb. moth eaten.
paragraphs.anchor: And my bones are consumed

paragraphs.text: Such as Shimei, who now insulted lustily; Leoni mortuo vel mus insultat.
paragraphs.anchor: I was a reproach among all mine enemies

paragraphs.text: My near allies and friends, such as Absalom and Ahithophel; these most vexed me.
paragraphs.anchor: But especially among my neighbours

paragraphs.text: It is no new thing that those which should most love men do sometimes, either for fear or flattery of others, make least account of them.
paragraphs.anchor: And a fear to mine acquaintance

paragraphs.text: They that did see me without (or, in the streets) fled from me] To shift for themselves; since to own me, whom they could not help, was bootless, and, besides, perilous.
How soon dead men are forgotten, even by those that promise to remember them longest of all, experience teacheth; trust not to protestations of best friends in that case.
paragraphs.anchor: I am forgotten as a dead man out of mind

paragraphs.text: Of which there is no further use or esteem.
paragraphs.anchor: I am like a broken vessel

paragraphs.text: Or, as Calvin, Mollerus, and others render it, magnorum, of the great ones, such as take counsel (so it followeth here), which the vulgar seldom do; and their tongues oft are no slander, as we say.
paragraphs.anchor: For I have heard the slander of many

paragraphs.text: Magormissabib, Pashur’s new name and doom, Jer 20:3-4; but good David’s condition at this time: without were fightings, within were fears.
paragraphs.anchor: Fear was on every side

paragraphs.text: See 2Sa 16:20, where we have an exposition of this verse. {See Trapp on "2Sa 16:20"}
paragraphs.anchor: While they took counsel together against me

paragraphs.text: In this distress I acted my faith upon thy power and promises; this was right, and that which God aimed at; for we can no way more honour him. Hence it is that he is very jealous of our trust; neither can he endure that any idol of jealousy should be set up in our hearts.
paragraphs.anchor: But I trusted in thee, O Lord

paragraphs.text: In nearest relation and dearest affection, whatever befalleth me.
paragraphs.anchor: I said, Thou art my God

paragraphs.text: Both the time of my abode on earth and all those various occurrences of that time, all is predetermined by thee; particularly how long I shall suffer, and when I shall be delivered. See 1Ch 29:30 Job 7:20.
paragraphs.anchor: My times are in thy hand

paragraphs.text: Oh command deliverances for me; for thou canst easily do it. And here observe how David riseth in his requests; he laid the covenant for a foundation, and then he well knew he might be bold to ask anything.
paragraphs.anchor: Deliver me from the hand of mine enemies

paragraphs.text: Which by reason of the clouds of affliction clustering about me, I cannot for present perceive. {See Trapp on "Psa 4:6"} {See Trapp on "Psa 30:7"}
paragraphs.anchor: Make thy face to shine, &c.

paragraphs.text: i.e. Deliver me out of these dangers.
paragraphs.anchor: Save me, &c.

paragraphs.text: i.e. Disappointed of my hopes.
paragraphs.anchor: Let me not be ashamed

paragraphs.text: For they call not upon God, but shame those that do, Psa 14:4; Psa 14:6.
paragraphs.anchor: Let the wicked be ashamed

paragraphs.text: Let their large spoken mouths be stopped with a spadeful of mould.
paragraphs.anchor: Let them be silent in the grave

paragraphs.text: Heb. the lips of a lie, mendaciorum artifices, as Jer 9:3; Jer 9:5. Among the Persians it was αιχιστον το φευδεσθαι, held a base shame to tell a lie. Oh that it were so among Christians! When shall that golden age return, that the argument may again proceed, Sacerdos est, non fallet; Christianus est, non mentietur; He is a minister, he will not deceive; he is a Christian, therefore he will not lie? (Herod. in Clio; Xenoph. Cyroep.; Strab. lib. 15).
paragraphs.anchor: Let the lying lips be put to silence

paragraphs.text: Heb. a hard thing; dura et atr ociaverba, durable and longlasting reproaches, such as stick, and leave a scar, though the wound be healed up. Calumniare audacter, aliquid saltem adhaerebit. Such mouths shall one day smoke for it, Jdg 1:15.
paragraphs.anchor: Which speak grievous things

paragraphs.text: Heb. In pride and contempt. It is pride that causeth contempt of others. Compare Pro 3:34 1Pe 5:5. David elsewhere complaineth of proud, rhetorical mockers.
paragraphs.anchor: Proudly and contemptuously

paragraphs.text: The prophet venteth himself by way of exclamation, as finding it unspeakable; fitter to be believed than possible to be discoursed; words are too weak to utter it. What shall we say to these things? quoth that great apostle, Rom 8:31.
paragraphs.anchor: Oh how great is thy goodness

paragraphs.text: Heb. hidden. Besides that good which God worketh openly for his before the sons of men, a great part of his wonderful kindness is hidden from the world, and in part also from themselves, both in respect of the fountain, 1Jn 3:1-2 Col 3:3, the fulness, 1Co 2:9, and the inward sealing up thereunto, 1Co 2:11-12 Rev 2:17 Pro 14:10.
paragraphs.anchor: Which thou hast laid up

paragraphs.text: For faith must be actuated; and when we have such a precious promise as this we must suck and be satisfied, Isa 66:11, put on to get the goodness of God to work, which is done by believing. Catch hold, as David did, 1Ch 17:23-26; and make the utmost of God’s loving-kindness laid up in a promise; press it, and oppress it, till the goodness be expressed out of these breasts of consolation.
paragraphs.anchor: For them that fear thee; that trust in thee

paragraphs.text: In the golden cabinet of thy gracious providence, where they shall be as safe as if they were in heaven.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy presence

paragraphs.text: A kind of speech taken from princes’ retiringrooms and withdrawing chambers, which are sacred places (Diodati).
paragraphs.anchor: Thou shalt keep them secretly in a pavilion

paragraphs.text: From the calumnies and contumelies of graceless tongue-smiters. The Arabic rendereth it, from the insurrection of tongues. Sedition is first in the tongue, and then in the hand; an unruly tongue setteth on fire, Jas 3:5 But the saints have a promise that as no weapon formed against them shall prosper, so every tongue that riseth against them in judgment shall be condemned, Isa 54:17.
paragraphs.anchor: From the strife of tongues

paragraphs.text: This should always be in a Christian’s mouth, as Deo gratias was in Austin’s. He can never want matter, and should, therefore, ever find a heart.
paragraphs.anchor: Blessed be the Lord

paragraphs.text: Mirificavit bonitatem suam, hath been far better to me than my hopes.
paragraphs.anchor: For he hath shewed me his marvellous kindness

paragraphs.text: In Mahanaim, 2Sa 18:27, where it is likely he made this and some other psalms.
paragraphs.anchor: In a strong city

paragraphs.text: A frightful and sinful saying, doubtless, full of diffidence and despair. See the like Psa 116:11 Job 9:16 Jdg 13:22 Psa 77:1-3; Joh 2:4. Thus he spake when he, trembling, fled, and was posting away.
paragraphs.anchor: For I said in my haste, I am cut off, &c.

paragraphs.text: A pitiful poor one though it were, and full of infirmity. God considereth whereof we are made; he taketh not advantages against his suppliants; it would be wide with them if he should.
paragraphs.anchor: Nevertheless thou heardest the voice of my supplication

paragraphs.text: Let not your hasty discontent beget in you hard thoughts of God or heavy thoughts against yourselves, as it hath done in me; but love him, trust him, and he will do you right.
paragraphs.anchor: O love the Lord

paragraphs.text: Heb. repayeth abundantly, or with surplus, in seipso vel in semine suo. It may be rendered, Upon the remainder, and understood of the proud man’s posterity, wherein God will be sure to meet with him.
paragraphs.anchor: And plentifully rewardeth

paragraphs.text: Bear up, be stout, and steadfast in the faith under trials. See Psa 27:14, with the note. Thus good courage cometh not but from the true love of God, Psa 31:23.
paragraphs.anchor: Be of good courage, &c.
